t: The Corded Ware culture is named after the cord-like impressions on its pottery, and its other names, Single Grave and Battle Axe culture, come from its burials and its men's grave goods.
Ancient DNA shows its people shared much of their ancestry with the Yamnaya culture of the steppe, though whether they descended from the Yamnaya themselves is still argued.
It is considered a likely vector for the spread of many Indo-European languages in Europe.
dyk: About 3,000 battle axes have been found across Scandinavia in Battle Axe culture graves, and archaeologists think they were above all objects of status.
ev: The earliest radiocarbon dates for Corded Ware come from Kujawy and Lesser Poland, though they are disputed
Corded Ware appears more or less at once in a number of centres across north central Europe
The Battle Axe culture appears in Denmark, Sweden and Norway
Corded Ware appears in Switzerland, where it lasts until 2400 BC
The Corded Ware horizon ends in the early Bronze Age

f.homeland: Most of continental northern Europe from the Rhine to the Volga, from Germany, the Netherlands and Denmark through Poland and the Baltic to northern Ukraine and European Russia, with coastal Norway and southern Sweden and Finland; sites include Bronocice, Eulau, Esperstedt, Zeewijk and Turinge
f.period: c. 2900–2300 BC, from the Late Neolithic through the Copper Age to the early Bronze Age; in Switzerland, dated by dendrochronology, only from 2750 to 2400 BC; regional groups include the Middle Dnieper, Fatyanovo–Balanovo, Single Grave, Scandinavian Battle Axe (from c. 2800 BC) and Finnish Battle Axe cultures
f.known: pottery decorated with twisted cord; single burial under small mounds in a crouched position; stone battle axes as men's grave goods; wheeled vehicles; steppe ancestry shared with the Yamnaya; a likely role in spreading Indo-European languages
f.sources: Named by Friedrich Klopfleisch in 1883; the Single Grave culture defined by Andreas Peter Madsen; mostly known from burials; ancient DNA studies including Haak et al. (2015), Allentoft et al. (2015), Saag et al. (2017) and Papac et al. (2021)
